title: Stress Management, Teamwork, and Conflict Management

unit.title: Program Orientation, Professionalism, and Healthcare Roles

sections.learningObjectives:
- Identify healthy ways to manage workplace stress.
- Describe effective teamwork and collaboration.
- Apply conflict-management strategies appropriately.
- Use professional communication during disagreement and recognize when to escalate conflicts.
- Recognize self-care as part of safe, sustainable medical office practice.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Stress is like a car's dashboard warning light. It just tells you something needs attention; it does not mean the driver is a bad driver.

### Question 2

Breaks are like pausing a long video game to stretch. A short pause helps you come back sharper instead of getting sloppy and frustrated.

### Question 3

If you keep dropping plates because your arms are full, you don't grab more plates; you set some down and ask for help. Same idea with too many tasks.

### Question 4

Venting to patients is like arguing with your family in front of guests; it makes everyone uncomfortable and does not fix the real problem.

### Question 5

When you are too sleepy to read a recipe, you don't guess the ingredients; you ask someone to help you read it. Fatigue means get help, not guess.

### Question 6

Slow breathing is like turning down the volume on a too-loud song so you can think clearly again.

### Question 7

When your backpack is too heavy, you take everything out and put it back in order. Listing and sorting tasks is like repacking your backpack.

### Question 8

Your body is like a phone battery. Sleep, movement, and good food keep it charged so it does not die in the middle of a busy day.

### Question 9

If a teammate on the soccer field looks hurt or sad, you check on them and help them get a coach. You don't announce it to the crowd.

### Question 10

If you cannot carry all the groceries in one trip, you tell someone and make two trips. You don't drop a bag on the stairs and walk away.

### Question 11

An EAP is like a school counselor for grown-ups at work; you can go talk privately and get help finding the right support.

### Question 12

Mindfulness is like really tasting your food instead of gulping it while watching TV; you notice what is happening right now.

### Question 13

Saying no when your plate is full is like not stacking a tenth pancake on top of nine; the tower just falls over.

### Question 14

Work-life balance is like keeping two balloons full: the 'work' balloon and the 'life' balloon both need air, or one goes flat.

### Question 15

When a teacher adds a big homework assignment, you ask which other homework can wait, instead of staying up all night.

### Question 16

When a smoke detector goes off, you get help right away; you don't just open a window. Repeated errors are the smoke alarm for stress.

### Question 17

Even a runner stops for water during a long race; pausing to recharge helps you keep going without collapsing.

### Question 18

A little excitement before a game can help you play well, but being worried and losing sleep every night for a month wears you down.

### Question 19

If two people call your name at once, you look at who needs help faster and wave a friend over to help the other. You don't ignore both.

### Question 20

Emotional exhaustion is like a phone that has been on 5% battery for weeks; it runs slower and can't do much before shutting down.

### Question 21

Talking to a friend about a rough day is like shaking out a wrinkled jacket; it smooths things out so you can wear it again tomorrow.

### Question 22

When you are tired and copying a phone number, you read it back digit by digit to be sure. Stress means double-check even more carefully.

### Question 23

Time off is like recharging a toy's batteries; you do fun, restful things so it runs well again.

### Question 24

Compassion fatigue is like a sponge that has soaked up so much that it can't hold any more water until it is wrung out.

### Question 25

A tidy desk is like a toolbox where every wrench has its spot; you find what you need without dumping everything out.

### Question 26

A medical office is like a restaurant: the cook, the server, and the host all work together so the customer has a great meal.

### Question 27

A sports team works because each player knows their position; the goalie doesn't also try to play striker.

### Question 28

If a teammate is struggling to carry boxes, you offer to grab one; you don't grab all of them silently or tattle to the coach.

### Question 29

A good handoff is like passing the baton in a relay race; you make sure the next runner has a firm grip before you let go.

### Question 30

Good communication is like a game of catch: you throw the ball and make sure the other person actually caught it.

### Question 31

Read-back is like repeating a friend's directions out loud so they can say 'yes, exactly' before you start driving.

### Question 32

You trust a friend who returns your stuff and keeps their promises; that is how trust is built at work too.

### Question 33

If your friend has spinach in their teeth, you whisper it; you don't shout it across the lunchroom.

### Question 34

An orchestra needs violins, drums, and flutes; each part matters even though they sound different.

### Question 35

The whole team is like a pit crew with one goal: get the car safely back on the track. Everyone's job serves that one goal.

### Question 36

When a new kid joins the team, you show them the drills and cheer them on; you don't leave them alone to figure it out.

### Question 37

Accountability is like returning a borrowed library book on time; you are responsible for it even if nobody reminds you.

### Question 38

If you don't know how to work a new tool, you ask someone to show you instead of pushing random buttons.

### Question 39

A good assistant is like a chef's helper who has the next ingredient ready before the chef asks.

### Question 40

Rolling your eyes while saying 'sure' sends the opposite message; your body talks even when your words don't.

### Question 41

Good feedback is like a coach saying 'keep your elbow up on the shot' rather than just yelling 'play better!'

### Question 42

Feedback is like a coach's tip to hold the bat differently; it helps you hit better, not an attack on you.

### Question 43

Documentation is like the shared whiteboard at a relay race; everyone can see who did what and what comes next.

### Question 44

Closed-loop is like ordering a pizza and repeating the toppings back so the shop confirms they got it right.

### Question 45

Gossip is like throwing mud; even if you are not the target, you get dirty by joining in.

### Question 46

Front and back office are like the kitchen and the waitstaff; the order only comes out right if they talk to each other.

### Question 47

Being flexible is like a player who can fill two positions when needed, not one who ignores the rules of the game.

### Question 48

If you disagree with the coach's play, you talk to the coach on the sidelines, not to the fans in the stands.

### Question 49

A good meeting is like a group puzzle; everyone adds their piece politely until the picture is complete.

### Question 50

If two people both start making the same sandwich, one finishes it while the other makes the drinks, so nothing is doubled and nothing is missed.

### Question 51

When two teammates argue, the first move is to talk it out on the sidelines, not to run to the referee or the crowd.

### Question 52

Active listening is like letting someone finish their turn in a board game before you roll; you understand their move first.

### Question 53

When roommates disagree about shelf space, they talk and split it fairly; they don't move each other's stuff in secret.

### Question 54

Saying 'I felt sad when...' is like saying 'this is how the game felt to me' instead of yelling 'you cheated!'

### Question 55

It is like fixing a leaky faucet by looking at the pipe, not calling the whole house 'broken.'

### Question 56

When a fire gets big, you don't throw more wood on it; you step back and let it cool before handling it.

### Question 57

If two players are arguing so much the game is falling apart, the coach has to step in. When care is affected, the supervisor steps in.

### Question 58

If you think a friend is mad, you ask them quietly instead of telling everyone and hiding from them.

### Question 59

Compromise is like two kids with one cookie agreeing to split it, so both get a fair piece.

### Question 60

When two players disagree on a rule, they check the rulebook, not a coin or whoever is older.

### Question 61

Talk about the spilled milk, not about how 'clumsy' the person is; the first fixes the problem, the second starts a fight.

### Question 62

When two kids can't solve a playground dispute, they ask a teacher, not another kid or a stranger.

### Question 63

Even when you are upset with a teammate, you still pass the ball during the game; the game comes first.

### Question 64

You don't argue with a teammate about the play in front of the audience; you take it to the locker room.

### Question 65

Collaboration is like building one big sandcastle together instead of two kids fighting over the same bucket.

### Question 66

If a pipe keeps leaking, you fix the pipe, not just mop the floor every time.

### Question 67

If a teammate keeps showing up late, you first tell them how it affects the game; if it keeps happening, you let the coach know.

### Question 68

Writing down what happened is like keeping the scorecard at a game; it keeps the facts straight when you later explain to the ref.

### Question 69

When you are really mad, you count to ten before talking; that pause stops you from saying something you can't take back.

### Question 70

A disagreement about a sticker is kid stuff, but if someone is about to break a window, you get an adult right away.

### Question 71

Say what you mean kindly and clearly, like asking for the salt at dinner, instead of making jokes or shouting.

### Question 72

Take turns talking, like passing the talking stick; everyone gets to finish their turn.

### Question 73

If you disagree with the referee, you ask to talk privately at halftime, not argue on the field in front of everyone.

### Question 74

You don't argue with your family in front of dinner guests; you save it for a private time.

### Question 75

Write an email like you are writing to a teacher: polite and clear, not in shouty capitals or while you're fuming.

### Question 76

Saying 'so you mean...?' is like double-checking a map before deciding you're lost.

### Question 77

If a teammate might hurt someone, you get the coach right away; you don't wait to see what happens.

### Question 78

If someone keeps pushing you on the playground, you tell the teacher; you don't keep it a secret.

### Question 79

If talking to your teammate didn't fix it, you take it to the coach; that's what the coach is for.

### Question 80

The chain of command is like knowing which teacher to ask first, then the principal, when a problem is too big.

### Question 81

If you see someone breaking the rules in a way that could hurt people, you tell a grown-up in charge right away.

### Question 82

Taking care of yourself is like charging your own battery so you have enough energy to help others plug in too.

### Question 83

A healthy boundary is like closing the bakery at night; the ovens cool down so they work again tomorrow.

### Question 84

If a cut won't heal and keeps hurting for weeks, you see a doctor; you don't just put another bandage on it.

### Question 85

Sustainable self-care is like brushing your teeth a little every day, not trying to clean them all at once once a year.
